slides.title: Decision Theory
slides.text:
Decision Theory
Decision theory is a field of study that deals with the principles and methods used to make decisions under various conditions of uncertainty.
The core idea is to provide a structured approach to making rational choices and optimising a certain objective, typically involving maximising utility or profit or minimising costs or risks.

slides.title: Conditions for applying quantitative techniques
slides.text:
Conditions for applying quantitative techniques
There must be alternatives to choose from.
The decision maker should be able to judge the likelihood of various possible consequences and should have a preference for each possible consequence.
The problem should conform to mathematical rationality.
The decision-making must be rational and consistent.
Source: Gupta and Khanna, “Quantitative Techniques for Decision Making” (4th Edition)

slides.title: Steps in Decision Making
slides.text:
Steps in Decision Making
List down all possible and available options. (Alternatives)
List down all the future events that can happen. (States of Nature)
Construct a Pay-Off Table, showing the payoff (in terms of profit, cost, time, etc.) resulting from each possible combination of alternatives and state of nature.
Source: Gupta and Khanna, “Quantitative Techniques for Decision Making” (4th Edition)

slides.title: Decision Making Environments
slides.text:
Decision Making Environments
Decision-making under certainty: There is only one outcome of decisions (state of nature) and it is known with certainty.
Decision-making under uncertainty: More than one state of nature, with unknown probabilities of occurrence.
Decision-making under risk: More than one state of nature, with known probabilities of occurrence.
Source: Gupta and Khanna, “Quantitative Techniques for Decision Making” (4th Edition)
OP5102 OPTIMIZATION TECHNIQUES

slides.title: Decision Making Criteria under Uncertainty
slides.text:
Decision Making Criteria under Uncertainty
Maximax Criterion: Choose the alternative that maximises the maximum payoff. (Optimistic Strategy)
Maximin Criterion: Choose the alternative that maximises the minimum payoff. (Conservative Strategy)
Minimax Regret Criterion: Choose the alternative that minimises the maximum regret, where regret is the difference between the payoff of the chosen alternative and the best possible payoff in each state of nature. [Savage’s Rule]
Expected Value Criterion: Calculate the weighted average of all possible outcomes using the probabilities of each state of nature. Choose the alternative with the maximum expected profit or minimum expected loss. This is often used for decision-making under risk.
Realism Criterion: It attempts to choose a middle ground between Maximax or Minimax Criterion. If the weights are based on varying probability of occurrence, then the Expected Value = α (Maximum Payoff) + (1- α)(Minimum Payoff) [Hurwicz’s Rule]
Criterion of Insufficient Reason: If it is assumed that all states of nature have an equal probability of occurrence, then the Expected Value = (1/n)(Outcome 1) + (1/n)(Outcome 2) + … + (1/n)(Outcome n) [Laplace’s Rule]
Source: Gupta and Khanna, “Quantitative Techniques for Decision Making” (4th Edition)
OP5102 OPTIMIZATION TECHNIQUES

slides.title: Decision Making under Risk
slides.text:
Decision Making under Risk
Decision-making under risk assumes that the decision-maker has sufficient information about the states of nature and the probabilities of their occurrences.
We calculate the expected values against those probabilities and choose the alternative with the highest expected payoff.

slides.title: Example 1
slides.text:
Example 1
A company is introducing a new product. It has the option of setting up a commercial plant now or setting up a pilot plant at present and setting up a commercial plant later, depending on the product’s performance. It has been estimated that the present cost of setting up the pilot plant will be ₹ 2 lakhs and the cost of setting up a commercial plant will be ₹ 21 lakhs. However, when the commercial plant is set up three months later, after observing the performance of the product, it will cost ₹ 25 lacs. It has also been estimated that the probability of the product giving a high yield during the pilot stage is 0.9 and that of giving a low yield is 0.1. If the product is introduced commercially without going through a pilot stage, it is expected that it will give a high yield of profits with a probability of 0.7. If the pilot plant does show a high yield, then the probability that the commercial plant will also give a high yield is 0.85; but if the pilot plant gives a low yield, the probability that the commercial plant will give a high yield is only 0.1. The estimated profit from the high yield at the commercial stage is ₹ 122.5 lakhs, and if the yield is low, the company will suffer a loss of ₹ 15.25 lakhs.
Draw the Decision Tree with the Expected Outcomes at each stage.
Find out the optimal decision out of the two alternatives: Build a Commercial Plant now or Start with a Pilot Plant Now, then go on building a Commercial Plant.
OP5102 OPTIMIZATION TECHNIQUES
